speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was saying that students, which number nearly a million Canadians, those in administrative positions and in the teaching faculties of unviversities and colleges, and researchers, all of whom total some 1.2 million Canadians in the field of post-secondary education, will be gravely affected by Bill C-96.
The Government has broken the promises it made to the Canadian people. The academic community, including students, teachers, professors and parents, asked what the Government would do in terms of the future of post-secondary education and whether it would maintain the agreement contained in the formula of 1977. The answer given by the Progressive Conservative Party was:
We are committed to sustaining the current federal financial commitment, according to the formula set out in the 1977 Agreement.
When asked if the Conservative Party supported the continuation of that agreement, the Conservatives said in different words:
Yes, we support fully the original 1977 funding formula and the legislation providing for that.
This legislation does not provide for that continuation, but for its destruction.
Unfortunately, the Party opposite has broken its promise to the electorate. It has broken its promise to the young people of this country in the future. Not only has the Government broken its promise in this legislation, it has also broken an agreement between the Canadian Government and the provinces. That was a solemn agreement on which the provinces counted to finance the health care and postsecondary institutions until March, 1987. The Government has broken that promise in mid-term and has cut off the increases which those provinces counted on to provide for medical care for Canadians and post-secondary education for our young people.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) originally stated that he would keep this promise. However, it is interesting to note that the Minister changed his mind after the banks collapsed in the West. He reversed his position and implemented this cut contained in Bill C-96. In other words, it appears to us, to the Canadian Association of University Teachers and to the academic community, that this Bill was introduced to help the
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
Government pay nearly $1 billion as a result of its decision on the bank's collapse in 1986. For the sake of supporting those who were in need of replacing the funds they had invested- some of whom were multi-millionaires-the Government took money away from the young people and gave it to the banks in which those people had deposits.
While I am not opposed to the Government taking that action, it should not be done at the expense of the young people of this country.
The Government broke its promise to the Canadian people, then proceeded to break an agreement between the Government of Canada and the provinces of this country. This year it will cut back on the anticipated revenues that the provinces expected for medical care and post-secondary education pursuant to an agreement that was supposed to end on March 1, 1987. That is a tragic mistake and a black mark on the Government's relationship with the provinces.
Furthermore, the Government has decided to move a closure motion in order to push this Bill through. The Government is limiting debate even though it has an enormous majority in the House. The Opposition totals only 70 Members out of 228. With that kind of majority I find it surprising that the Conservatives still feel it necessary to use their power to crush and prevent the Opposition from debating this Bill.
The provinces are not happy with this Bill. Premier after premier has accused the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Government of reducing the growth of federal funds for health and education without consultation. That is a scandal. As if there were not enough scandals now, the Government must muzzle the Opposition and prevent it from representing the provinces. There are at least eight provincial Governments which have formally and informally expressed their distaste about what the Government is doing with respect to postsecondary education and medical care of the Canadian people through Bill C-96. The Government told the provinces it was going to cut their funding but did not discuss it with them. The Government just announced the cuts. It was done by fiat. We know now what happened to the promise of dialogue and consultation.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada (Mr. Scott) said on April 25, and I quote from Hansard at page 12668:
No province will be affected any more or any less than any other province through this Bill.
What an outrageous remark, Mr. Speaker, when we know that some provinces are less well off economically than other provinces! How could anyone dare to say on behalf of the Provinces of Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Manitoba or Saskatchewan that they will be affected in just the same way as all other provinces? Terence Donahoe, the Minister of Human Resources Development and Training of Nova Scotia, a Tory provincial Government, is quoted in The Globe and Mail on January 28 as saying, and I quote:

May 8, 1986
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
-if Ottawa goes ahead with the reduction in grants it simply will emasculate the post-secondary education system. It is going to be chaos and chaotic. Regardless of whose numbers you are going to use, the system is simply going to fall apart.
Mr. Donahoe is a Minister in the Government of the Province of Nova Scotia and he is talking about the educational system of Nova Scotia. He is worried about one of the finest systems of education in Canada. These are not idle words. We should listen to the professors, the people who are running Dalhousie University and the people involved, whether it be students or faculty. We should listen to the CBC about the state of affairs at Dalhousie and we will understand why the Minister from Nova Scotia is talking not through his hat, but from his heart and knowledge as a Minister of the Crown of that province as to what will be the results of this Bill.
For the sake of the people of that province, if for no one else, I urge the Government to reconsider this Bill and not to try to muzzle us.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be very brief. As I understand, the main argument of members of the Government is that the $5 billion cut from the Established Programs Financing Act over the next five years is not a cut at all but in fact an increase. For the life of me, I cannot understand how on earth they can call a $5 billion reduction in transfer payments for medicare and post-secondary education from the federal Government to the provinces as an increase. It does not only escape logic, it does not jibe with the promises made by the Progressive Conservative Party to the Canadian people during the 1984 election campaign. What the Progressive Conservative Party said in its Campaign Handbook with respect to established programs financing was, and I quote:
We would return to the 1977 funding formula though we cannot compensate the provinces for their 6-and 5-funding losses. We will institute regular consultation with the provinces as set out in the original agreement to reach a consensus on national goals in post-secondary education.
As we know now, Mr. Speaker, the Government did not consult with the provinces and certainly did not follow through on the promises it made during the election campaign, not only with respect to this program but with respect to a whole host of other programs.
I can only Find one individual during this whole debate who has referred to the cuts as "cuts". The Hon. Member for the Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) quite forthrightly and honestly said, and I quote from Hansard of May 6, at page 12978:
It is always difficult to stand up in the House of Commons or anywhere else and defend cuts in health services,
So he is one member of the Government who recognizes that the Government is attacking the ability of the provinces to fulfil their commitments to medicare programs and postsecondary education. In the process, the Government will hurt an awful lot of Canadians who should have the right to equal access to medicare whether they live in Newfoundland, Labrador, British Columbia or anywhere else in the country. Rather than having one standard of health care services apply to all Canadians equally, Canadians will receive different
health care services depending in which part of the country they live in and on the ability of their particular province to deliver that health care service. Exactly the same thing will happen to the youth of this country, many of whom will be denied access to higher education simply because they cannot afford it. That is contrary to every principle which has been discussed in our country for many years. Access to quality education and health care is basic to our form of democracy.
I know my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton- East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall), has other pressing demands on his time, as we all do, so I will end my remarks to allow him to speak. To conclude I will simply say that what the Government is doing is the height of hypocrisy for which it will pay in the next election.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague, the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young) who, as usual, has displayed a great deal of knowledge on the subject matter we are debating. What is more important, I agree wholeheartedly with the substance of his remarks. I must say that this is quite remarkable in view of some of the positions which have been taken by other members of his caucus.
Bill C-96, an Act to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act, is very important. It is very important in the way in which the Government operates. It is important in the way in which the Government treats its various provinces and, in particular, the people who reside in those provinces.
I would like to ask the following question. Is this an open Government? The question has to be answered in the negative. In dealing with a piece of legislation as important as Bill C-96 one would have hoped that the Government would see fit not to invoke the provisions of closure but, perhaps, to allow a full and open debate on the effects this negative piece of legislation will have on the provinces. Unfortunately, that was not the choice of the Government. Its choice was to close debate by using the most Draconian measure Parliament has seen in many years, that is, closure.
I can see by your facial expression that you too, Mr. Speaker, are disappointed with the way in which members of the Government have conducted themselves with regard to the provisions of open government. Open government and stability are certainly not a part of this Government's actions in terms of Bill C-96.
The thrust of the Bill before us is to take away from the provinces monies earmarked for necessities. I refer to the necessities of health care and the necessities which our postsecondary institutions provide. The Government is attempting day by day to transfer the deficit of the nation to the provinces. It is not fair that the provinces are now being told that
May 8, 1986

they have to change their budget allocations for, perhaps, the two most important sectors of our economy.
When the provincial Premiers met in Halifax at the last First Ministers' Conference they said it very clearly and unequivocally. They said that they did not want cut-backs in transfer payments to take place. Many of those First Ministers had already planned and allocated monies for their various budgets in terms of health care and education. However, the Government, which had campaigned on this bid of consultation, has once again shown its true colours in that there has been no consultation. That has been said time and time again, not only by the Premiers of Ontario and Quebec but by Premiers of the same political stripe as this Government. I refer Hon. Members to the Premier of New Brunswick and to the First Minister of the Province of Newfoundland. If these measures go through, then these provinces will experience even more difficult times than those which confront them today.
I think I can share with you, Mr. Speaker, just what these cut-backs will mean to my region of Canada. In 1986-87, the reduction to the Province of Newfoundland will amount to $7.3 million. For the Province of Prince Edward Island the figure is $1.6 million. For New Brunswick it is $9 million, and for my Province of Nova Scotia it is $11.1 million. These are substantial reductions in two areas which every Government since the beginning of Confederation, both provincial and federal, has deemed to be the most important areas involving everyday Canadians. However, the Government, supported and abetted by those Members of Parliament who refuse to take their Government on, are saying to the Provinces of Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick that the quality of health care the citizens of those provinces have grown to live with will now be worse- substantially worse.
I know there are Members in the Chamber who will say that my comment is one of a partisan nature. However, individual after individual, whether it be the representative from the provincial medical society of New Brunswick, or others, have come before our caucus and shared with us how these cutbacks will affect not only the medical society but the health care of the people of New Brunswick. In the outlying regions of the Province of New Brunswick individuals are without health care. They are without the opportunity which Canadians in every other province deem to be their right. They have been left without those services. We are now saying to them that we will cut them back even more. The situation in the Provinces of New Brunswick and Newfoundland is similar in that these cuts will be very substantial.
In 1987-88, the reduction for the Province of Newfoundland will amount to $15.5 million. For the Province of Prince Edward Island it will be $3.4 million, and $1.2 million for New Brunswick. For my Province of Nova Scotia it will be $23.6 million.
One must underline the importance of transfer payments. They were introduced not at the whim and prayer of some politician on the hustings at the time, but after major studies
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
affecting all of Canada were debated in the House of Commons, in the provincial legislatures and by the public at large. These discussions were to the effect that there was a pressing need for services in education and health care to be equal across the country. They are no longer equal. In the Province of Nova Scotia any individual in post-secondary education today will tell us that he or she is being cut to the bone. To impose additional reductions on these people will make it virtually impossible for them. It will be asking them to row a boat without oars. The situation is becoming extremely difficult in the Atlantic provinces with our diverse and small population there. Nonetheless, it is a population which wants to be educated and wants to have the same opportunities as other regions of the country have. Whether or not we consider the urban centres of Toronto or Montreal, we want the same rights.
These cut-backs will hit the very fibre of the country, something which has been echoed by Premier Pawley of Manitoba. That is what he said at the First Ministers' Conference. He said that they cannot make any more cuts. I hope that, not because of political partisanship on the part of Members opposite or because they want to be politically blind to the realities of 1986, they will take it upon themselves either to visit post-secondary institutions or to view, as I have done firsthand, the various medical services which are not available to rural communities. I am certain that any reasonable man or woman after seeing firsthand what is actually out there will agree that Bill C-96 is discriminatory both in substance and in terms of the effects it will have on all regions of the country.
A former Prime Minister who made an analogy with regard to language and how important it was for Canada to adopt two official languages also said that if regional disparities are not stopped and reversed they are more likely than anything else to destroy the country.
Bill C-96 cuts back on funds going to the Province of Prince Edward Island. In view of the recent election results from that province, I am astounded that Conservative Members of Parliament have not realized that people there do not like the type of Government they are getting under the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
I will conclude by saying this, not for partisanship but for the real benefit of all Canadians wherever they may live: we ought to vote down the provisions of Bill C-96 because it is a Bill that is discriminatory, unfair and un-Canadian.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has taken two years longer than we expected to get to the world of George Orwell. It has taken until 1986, but we now have a Government which is trying to call black white and white black. We have a Government which is in fact severely, dangerously and at extreme human cost cutting back the amount of money the provinces expected to receive to pay for very basic human services. Yet this measure is being described by the Government, and particularly the Minister of Finance

May 8, 1986
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act
(Mr. Wilson), as not being a cut but simply a reduction in the rate of growth. When a province has budgeted for certain increases, reduction in the rate of growth is in fact, in practice and in reality a cut to the amount expected and required to pay for the needs of the people of the province.
What I think is so particularly sad about the action taken by the Government with respect to the established programs financing is that it runs directly counter to what the Government said it intended to do when Conservative Members ran for election in 1984. According to the Conservative Campaign Handbook of 1984 in which, as usual, the Conservatives attacked the Liberals and New Democrats for their inadequacies, the Conservatives said very clearly that it was the PC position that they would return to the 1977 funding formula although they could not compensate the provinces for their funding losses under the 6-and 5-program. They also said that they would institute regular consultation with the provinces as set out in the original agreement to reach a consensus on national goals.
Those remarks referred to post-secondary education, just one of the set of programs with which Bill C-96 deals, but very clearly that makes the point that the Conservative Party promised to turn around the past attempt to squeeze the provinces and, instead, offer increases which would keep up with the increase in the Gross National Product and therefore provide the provinces with the financial mechanisms required to fill the crucial needs of the people in the fields of education and medical care and to fill the other basic needs for which federal financing provides.
What is the reality as opposed to the promises made by Conservative Members before they were elected? The reality is that Bill C-96, instead of bringing a return to fairness, predictability and consensus with the provinces, has brought an increase in the slash-and-cut technique for which the Conservatives blamed the Liberals prior to the 1984 election. Conservative Members were right to blame the Liberals for that kind of slash-and-burn technique. They are wrong now to adopt that technique and to put into effect what amounts to, first, a complete break from their own promises and, second, a reproduction of past Liberal mistakes.
In reality, as a result of this Bill, there will be a tremendous decrease in the funding available to the provinces to meet basic human needs. Under the old formula which is in existence at the moment, the provinces expected to receive roughly $97.7 billion in federal contributions between 1986 and 1991. The new formula which Bill C-96 will put into effect will provide roughly $92.1 billion. One does not have to be a mathematical whiz to see that a cut of more than $5 billion has been imposed on the provinces.
I say to the Conservative back-benchers who represent Ontario that they should be protesting against this Bill particularly strongly. The cuts under this Bill will hit Ontario in larger measure than any other province. According to our statistics, over five years, in excess of $2 billion will be cut back from the amount of money the Province of Ontario would
have expected to receive from the federal Government in order to pay for basic post-secondary education costs and medical care.
We might ask ourselves why it is that the Province of Ontario faces a serious crisis in health care. This was shown by the protests of doctors and medical personnel which were heard yesterday in Toronto. Why is that crisis in health care being experienced? Why is a crisis in funding for postsecondary education being experienced? Students and university professors have spoken to our committee and other committees about that crisis. The answer is very clear. It is because of the slash-and-burn technique which Conservative Members are now putting into effect in the name of some kind of crazy deficit reduction which is occurring on the backs of the ordinary people of Canada. It is not fair, it is not just and it should not be permitted in a federal system. There should be a bond of faith in the federal system between the federal Government and the provinces that they are guaranteed a set amount of money on which they can count.
We have here a Bill which not only breaks promises to the people of Canada but also breaks faith with the whole federal system in which the Government claims to have such great faith and belief. It is, in short, Mr. Speaker, an example of how badly misguided this Conservative Government has become in the less than two years since it took office.
For myself I have to say that it is with great regret that I see Bill C-96 brought before this House of Commons for it represents the destruction of the faith people had in a change of Government and what that change might have brought about.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND FEDERAL POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND HEALTH CONTRIBUTIONS ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-96 has to do with what we call the established programs financing arrangements which are negotiated between the federal Government and the provinces of Canada. It is called EPF for short and it deals with health and post-secondary education. The reason we have EPF is very simple. It was decided a long time ago that what we wanted in this country was to have nationally acceptable standards in health care and education. What we are doing with Bill C-96 is changing an established programs funding into a destabilized programs funding. We are destabilizing the program. Instead of EPF it is DPF.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has offered a rationale for Bill C-96. It goes something like this. What we have at the present time is a runaway deficit. The impact of this runaway deficit is far greater than that of shifting it to the provinces. That is the Minister's argument. Let us consider that for a moment. I do not think we can disagree with the Minister of Finance that we do have a runaway deficit for that is hard to argue against. It is hard to say that the deficit is not a serious national problem. It is so serious that in the very near future, in the early 1990s, we may be spending 50 cents on every tax dollar collected just to pay the interest on the
May 8, 1986

national debt. What happens when that figure reaches 75 per cent or 90 per cent? It is obvious that most Government departments would be irrelevant. They will no longer be required. Parliament itself will not have much of a function. We would probably need only one government Department and one government agency. We would need Taxation Canada to collect the money and transfer it to the Bank of Canada, which would disburse it to those people who were fortunate enough to own government bonds of one kind or another or treasury bills. That is what would be called the Government of Canada,.
The situation is serious and I have to agree with the Minister that the deficit is serious. What we need is a national program. We need all political Parties, all publicly-elected people from the municipal through the provincial and federal level, to co-operate to do something about our burgeoning national debt.
That brings me back to Bill C-96. Is it really the answer, as proposed by the Minister of Finance, simply to take a portion of the federal deficit and transfer it to the provinces? I find that very difficult to accept as a reasonable solution, but not all Hon. Members agree with me.
For example, yesterday or the day before the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Minaker), who is a government supporter and a former member of the Manitoba Legislature, argued that the provinces have some responsibility for restraining their expenditures. I found that argument a bit puzzling. I am not aware, and I certainly stand to be corrected, of a single province that is not taking some action to restrain its own expenditures. I think there is a consciousness in all of the provincial capitals that they must do what they can do to control their own deficits.
The Member for Winnipeg-St. James went on to argue that with Bill C-96 we are not cutting back at all because there will still be increases. He argued that there will not be decreases, there will be increases, so really there are no cutbacks.
That is a fatuous argument. We know there is in place now an agreement between the provinces and the federal Government. I thought these agreements were binding, but apparently they can be broken arbitrarily. They can be broken unilaterally. That bothers me because the Party opposite now in power argued that that should not be done. More than that I am bothered because two aspects of our national life, postsecondary education and health, will certainly suffer as a result of Bill C-96.
I would like to ask Members on the government side whether they believe that post-secondary education in Canada is overfunded. Is post-secondary education receiving an unduly large share of the amount of financial resources that are available? I took a careful look at that matter, and discovered that from 1977 to 1985 there was a very large increase in the enrolment, 27 per cent in our universities, over that period of
Criminal Code
time. In the colleges, the increase was even more significant, that is, 36 per cent.
How much additional funds flowed from the federal Government during that period of time to offset the increases? Government support increased by only 2.5 per cent. I am talking here about an actual increase. We have to take into account inflation. You cannot add that in because it means that higher salaries to keep up with inflation and operating costs of universities and colleges have to match inflation. This was an actual increase over and above inflation of 2.5 per cent, but it does not square with the increased demands placed on our post-secondary institutions.
Mr. Ed Anderson, President of the Canadian Association of University Teachers, said:
Proposed federal cuts to post-secondary education could place a university education beyond the reach of many students.
There is a basic problem with Bill C-96. It is unfair, it is arbitrary and, if I can conclude with just a short quote, let me say that I agree with The Telegraph Journal which wrote:
It is essential that the deficit be reduced and it is essential that the burden of the deficit be spread fairly across Canada and all regions of Canada. What the federal Government is doing does not ensure such fairness in the sharing of the burden.
The Telegraph Journal wrote this with respect to Bill C-96.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT RESPECTING LEGAL COUNSEL FOR UNBORN CHILD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-254 which I consider to be a very important Bill in that it deals with the protection of the unborn child. I believe that if the proposed amendment to the Criminal Code were adopted we would see a strengthening of the protection of the unborn child.
As a Member, I have chosen to speak on this Bill because I think it is very important. It is a subject which evokes very strong feelings in most Canadians. I am sure that my rising to speak on the Bill will cause concern for some of my constituents who will disagree with my views. Nevertheless, I feel a

May 8, 1986
Criminal Code
responsibility to do all 1 can to protect innocent, helpless, human life. Human life is sacred because it comes from God and, therefore, I feel that as a legislator I must act to defend innocent human beings, including the unborn.
In my opinion, abortion is not an acceptable alternative to the inconvenience of pregnancy. However, if the life or health of a mother is threatened and an operation which cannot be avoided results in the death of an unborn child, that is acceptable as long as the intent of the operation was to maintain life rather than to kill.
I believe that free, strong countries cannot survive or prosper if Governments lack the moral courage to protect innocent, helpless people. For this reason I feel that our country should not only protect the unborn child, but that Canada should also attempt to set an example for other countries, which have liberalized their abortion laws and customs, to follow. Someone must stand up for the unborn since they cannot do so themselves. The responsibility to support life vigorously rests with this House.
1 am told that in my own province many women travel to other provinces or the United States each month to obtain abortions. It is unfortunate that unwanted pregnancies occur in the first place, and I am among the first to support the need for more sex education programs which would prevent such things from happening. I also suggest that our churches should increase their activities with regard to family life and sex education. I see education as an alternative to continued criminalization of the abortion procedure and imposition of government sanctions. However, these appear to be necessary in the short run.
Some people would have us believe that most countries in the world have liberalized their abortion laws to the point where abortion on demand is permitted at the unconditional request of the woman. In fact, this is not the case. Only 10 countries in the world permit unconditional abortions. Some countries, including Ireland, the Philippines, and Portugal provide absolutely no exemption from absolute prohibition of abortion, even for the narrow purpose of saving the mother's life.
Some people would have us believe that most women believe that abortion is morally acceptable. However, a poll taken by Life magazine in 1983 indicates that 56 per cent of women polled believe it is morally wrong. It is also interesting to note the policy of the Canadian Medical Association. A policy document of that association indicates that the CMA is "opposed to abortion on demand or the use of the procedure as a method of birth control emphasizing the importance of counselling services, family planning facilities, and services and access to contraceptive information".
This matter has often been raised in the House in the past. Many present and former Members have had some very interesting things to say on the subject. I think it would be worthwhile for me to review some of the comments made in
recent years. Mr. Bill Yurko, the former Member for Edmonton East, introduced two Private Members' Bills in the House dealing with the subject of abortion. On November 18, 1980, in the House of Commons he said:
This is not a partisan issue. It is a moral issue of profound importance. It is an issue upon which each individual must reflect and make up his own mind.
I have always lived by the philosophy that it is my duty to protect, enhance, improve, cherish and embrace human life in all its dimensions. I have always asked myself the fundamental question: what is human life?
He goes on to say:
-in my estimation human life is a unique form of intelligence. At conception this intelligence is programmed and it evolves with the simple provision of an environment and a means of feeding. It is totally programmed, it is human life right after the moment of conception.
The Member for	Kindersley-Lloydminster	(Mr. McKnight), who is now the Minister of Labour, spoke in debate on Bill C-216 in the House of Commons on that same date. He said:
Bill C-216 is simple and straightforward. Its intention is to erase the loophole which literally permits abortion on demand and to ensure that the unborn child receives the full protection of the law and to repeal the section of the Criminal Code which allows therapeutic abortion committees to be formed.
He went on to say:
Although the issue of abortion is emotional, it is one upon which we cannot be silent. Since the abortion law was put in place 11 years ago, over 450,000 innocent children, human beings, have been killed.
We cannot be shrill or strident; we must be rationale and have certain expections of the people of Canada. In each and every one of us there is the emotion to recognize humanity. Humanity has many definitions. The definition which I in my own mind and conscience accept is that of the human being, whether it be a human being outside the womb or a human being in the womb.
On January 19, 1981, the Hon. Member for Richmond- South Delta (Mr. Siddon), who is now the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, quoted some StatsCan statistics which indicated
-a further alarming increase in the use of abortion as a means of population control-
He noted that:
-18 innocent children were sacrificed by abortion last year for every 100 live births, with 34 abortions to every 100 live births in my Province of British Columbia alone.
He went on to move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) and endorsed by many Members of the House:
That this House stand in silence for two minutes, in memory of the 65,135 innocent Canadian human infants whose lives were taken away by abortion during the past year; and furthermore this House admits, to its shame, that these acts have been taken with the consent of the Government of Canada.
There was obviously a great deal of concern expressed there, Mr. Speaker. I would also like to quote a Member of this House for whom I have a great deal of respect. On October 17, 1983, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) made a statement with regard to abortion. In speaking about Dr. Henry Morgentaler's abortion clinic he quoted a Toronto newspaper story which read in part: "Dr. Henry Morgentaler will defy the law and reopen his Toronto abortion clinic-". He said:
May 8, 1986

I can see nothing noble about this man breaking and defying the laws of Canada. Abortions to protect the life of the mother are legal today, but Dr. Morgentaler wants abortion on demand. He wants abortion to be a birth control measure, and he thinks freedom of choice should be extended to allow for the murder of another human being-yes, even an unborn child.
He went on to say:
World famous scientists like Professor A. W. Liley of Aukland, New Zealand, confirm that what is in the womb is "a person, a full human being that can cry, hiccup, dream, kick, suck a thumb, take "food", regulate fluid volume, have heart beats and fingerprints-a totally separate individual who stops his mother's periods and who decides when labour should begin".
Murder is murder, whether it occurs before birth or after birth. If we permit unborn and so-called unwanted babies to be killed, the next step may be to permit the killing of the crippled, the abnormal and the aged.
Many other Hon. Members have spoken on this issue in this House with much more authority and experience than I have. I certainly endorse the remarks and previous statements made by speakers in debate on this very important issue. 1 wish the Hon. Member success with his Bill because I think this is one of the most critical and important basic issues with which the House of Commons will be faced in future years.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT RESPECTING LEGAL COUNSEL FOR UNBORN CHILD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed an honour to rise and speak on Bill C-254, an Act to amend the Criminal Code to provide legal counsel for the unborn child at meetings of therapeutic abortion committees.
A Bill such as this is fraught with difficulties, even, I venture to say, insurmountable difficulties. To begin with, I am very reluctant to support legislation which would force costs of a substantial nature upon the provinces. The Minister of Social Services for each province, who is responsible for the provision of counsel under this Bill, is I am sure endeavouring to restrain or reduce costs in his or her department at a time of fiscal restraint. The expense of providing highly-paid legal counsel would be prohibitive. Even if one were to deflect this with the notion that legal aid could provide counsel, it must be realized that legal aid is also paid for by the taxpayer. My understanding is that the federal Government, through the Department of Justice, shares the cost of providing criminal legal aid. Through the Department of National Health and Welfare it shares the cost of some civil legal aid as an item of need under the Canada Assistance Plan. I also note that provincial plans are under the jurisdiction of provincial Ministers of Justice, not Ministers of Social Services. No matter which plan offers legal aid, however, there is a fundamental threshold of eligibility, both financial and legal, and those standards are determined by the individual provinces.
How would one determine the eligibility of the fetus for legal aid? Do we simply provide legal aid across the board? Free counsel for all? If so, what about the provision of legal counsel for the individual carrying the fetus? It must be assumed that representation for the unborn will turn the committee into an adversarial arena, with mother and fetus in an adversarial relationship. As well, the rules of natural justice would seem to require that if the state provides free legal counsel to one party without regard to financial eligibility, it
Criminal Code
must do the same for the other party as well. In addition, I can see the argument arising that the father and other family members should also be allowed to intervene in these proceedings with counsel, as well as other interested parties such as social service agencies. If I were a doctor sitting on one of those committees I would most certainly wish to have counsel advise me as well. Who is going to pay for all this?
Apart from the matter of the expense of state intervention, there are other, equally serious ramifications involved in this proposed amendment. As currently set out in the Criminal Code of Canada, the therapeutic abortion committee is to be comprised of three medical doctors. If this proposed amendment were to pass, we would be asking medical practitioners to hear and determine points of law. They are not qualified to do that. In the parlance of administrative law we would be asking the medical profession to make judicial or quasi judicial decisions. Apart from the sheer improbabilty and impropriety of such a move, by turning the procedure into a judicial hearing the rules of natural justice will come into play. No longer will the committee consist of medical practitioners reaching a medical determination. The addition of counsel and legal argument and the rules of natural justice mean the incorporation of the right to notice, the right to a fair hearing, the right to be heard, and the inclusion of a plethora of case law or precedents which have been developed in this area over the years. I can envision a backlog of cases which, in all likelihood, could strike at the very fundamental right to be heard.
We must remember that time is of the essence in these matters. Delay due to preliminary motions or adjournments or other common legal procedures could strike at the very heart of the therapeutic abortion committee. Delays could result in a pregnancy going beyond the vital first trimester where a necessary abortion can be safely performed. As well, it would seem that further amendments might be required in order to place persons on the committee who are knowledgeable enough to deal with the inevitable legal arguments this proposed amendment invite. In short, the Bill proposes to change in a fundamental way the very nature of the committee as it is now set out in the Criminal Code.
We easily speak of rights in this day and age, but we must be careful to remember that rights laid down in legislation are absolute and lead to rules, regulations and bureaucracy, and can therefore lead to obstruction of the desired outcome. We cannot fiddle or tinker with the law and not expect that to lead often to greater complexity.
My final point of concern relates to the actual administration of this proposed scheme. What procedures will be put in place to effect representation for the unborn? Will there be a panel of lawyers available? How will they be selected? Given the wide difference of opinion in our society on the abortion issue, one can assume that a range of opinion is present within the legal profession. Will this work be available only to lawyers who are philosophically opposed to or supportive of abortion? Even if the bar maintains its neutrality in acting for the

May 8, 1986
Criminal Code
unborn regardless of personal opinion, how does counsel receive instructions? Will it somehow be deemed they are to oppose the abortion automatically? If counsel cannot receive instructions from the client, is it his or her opinion which will be put forward? If counsel must be opposed, what would happen in cases of a pregnancy resulting from rape or incest?
The argument over abortion will continue. There will never be unanimity of opinion. The current section of the Criminal Code is a result of long study and a solid compromise with which most Canadians appear to agree. While the issue will continue to be the subject of debate, and while I commend the Hon. Member for his effort and concern in this area, the proposed amendment is too flawed to be put forward at this time.

speechtext: There are a number of those.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT RESPECTING LEGAL COUNSEL FOR UNBORN CHILD
speechtext:
There are a number of those involved as well. I mean the time honoured and well-respected legal profession. What do they call it, the second oldest profession? We barristers and solicitors know we are, if not the first, the second oldest profession, at least among solicitors. I will not mention the other solicitors out there.
Before I get into the content of this Bill I want to tell you a little story concerning lawyers. There was a cruise ship off the Bahamas last winter. There was a businessmen's convention in progress on board and there were two lawyers there. They were arguing about a legal point. The argument got so heated, rather like those of the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) sometimes here in the House of Commons or in the committees, that the lawyers fell overboard into the shark-infested waters. Immediately a bunch of sharks came up, but they suddenly formed a line and the two lawyers were able to swim right back to the boat. The businessman said: "That was a miracle". One of the wives of the lawyers looked over and said: "No, that is not a miracle, that was just professional courtesy". It seems to me that this is what is often thought of lawyers. The reason I mentioned it in connection with this Bill is that this is a Bill that for the first time goes beyond birth to get that ancient profession once again involved. I wondered when I was a lawyer how fortunate I was because I could go beyond death on the other end. I could send my bill not to the poor client, who was already gone, but I could send it to his or
her estate. I could collect from the estate, and it was all very nice. You could go beyond death.
They say you cannot take it with you, but lawyers can get it from you after you have gone by doing all the work, handling the estate. Each province has a Wills Act, death duties and probating wills. If you die without a will, you still have lawyers who have to put you through a process called dying intestate, without a will. You have to go to court, make an application, and you incur legal bills. What this Private Member's Bill, does, while it is well intentioned, is to involve lawyers now before birth. When the poor kid comes out, you could sort of, if I can put it that way, give it a lawyer's bill. So you are born, and what do you get? You get a lawyer's bill. What a way to face the earth.
I must say I have mixed opinions about that. I do not want to make fun of this. I personally would benefit from it, as would my colleagues, the barristers and solicitors of this country, who would be quite pleased to be able to submit a bill. It is quite possible that you could have, with this Bill, someone coming into the world owing money to a lawyer who appeared before an abortion committee. I know that is extending it a little, and I know the Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) would perhaps want me to be more serious in dealing with this.
Let me get away from lawyers and talk a little bit more about the Bill. The Hon. Member who last spoke, my colleague and friend from Maritime Canada, raised some interesting points. A good point he made was, how would counsel get instructions? They obviously do not get it from the fetus. They have to get it from somewhere. Do they oppose the abortion? Do they agree to the abortion? What if there is medical evidence to say the fetus, when born, will be born with Down's syndrome or with another handicapping disease, or will be born with permanent mental or brain damage? Those things can be discovered now. What if that is the situation? Does the lawyer take the position that, as counsel on behalf of the fetus, he is arguing that the fetus should be aborted? That is possible, I think, under this particular Bill. Perhaps some of the other Members will show me how this would not happen. I think that is what the Member who last spoke was getting at, by saying that, in spite of the intention of the Bill, there are a lot of questions that remain to be answered.
How does Legal Aid choose a lawyer? Presumably the lawyers are professionals and they would argue the matter properly. Even that is difficult. Who is your client? Is your client the family? The mother? The mother wants the abortion, presumably. Is your client one of these crazies like Joe Borowski, one of these kinds of people? Is that your client? Is your client like people who go around hitting people over the head in front of Doctor Morgentaler's clinic? Is that who you have to listen to?
Members of this House know how difficult the abortion issue is. Can you imagine some poor lawyer, in his first case, when he goes to the abortion committee having to go through a
May 8, 1986

picket line of pro or anti-abortionists? It would be absurd. It is not hard to indicate some of the difficulties here.
The Member mentioned the possibility of a rape case or an incest case. This is another example where, if I were counsel in the case, I would probably want to argue the possibility of abortion. It raises some fundamental issues about taking instructions, what kind of instructions, and even theorizing what a handicapped fetus would want. There are arguments on many sides here.
The Member who last spoke also talked about the current law on therepeutic abortions and the doctors' committee. I do not know if he heard a person I very much enjoy listening to on the radio, Mr. Peter Gzowski of Morningside on CBC Radio, but he had the other day women doctors on the program who were talking about their patients, women who wanted abortions. They talked about the terrible delays these women were having with the present system. I know the Member who last spoke said the present system is acceptable. I do not believe it is acceptable. These doctors were recounting how their patients were suffering, and that what would have been a simple matter, in terms of a medical operation for an abortion, became much more complicated as the matter was delayed for a number of weeks. It made it harder for the operation, it made it more difficult medically. Irrespective of what you want to argue on the abortion matter, the evidence that they gave was irrefutable, there was a problem with the delay in getting an abortion.
Would this Bill, and the appointment of a counsel-and again I say we lawyers look for business anywhere we can get it-but to be honest, does this not raise a lot of problems in terms of the potential for even further delay? A lawyer needs time to consult, time to prepare a brief and so on. What would happen is that there would be no abortion. That is really what would happen.
Maybe the inarticulated major premise behind this is that they really do not want any abortions at all. It is not a Bill about legal counsel for the unborn child. Then we are back to the days of abortions in the back alleys. I think I have made my point, which is the difficulties of having counsel in such a situation. I cannot help noting that Shakespeare certainly would not approve of this because he wanted to get rid of the lawyers, and now this Bill would get them not only after death, but even before birth.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT RESPECTING LEGAL COUNSEL FOR UNBORN CHILD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this important debate on Bill C-254. Before commencing my remarks I would just like to clarify briefly the purpose of the legislation, at least on paper. The Bill requires that every fetus be represented by counsel at a meeting of the therapeutic abortion committee. In my view, Mr. Speaker, while one examines this Bill, and on the face of it it is an Act to amend the Criminal Code to provide for legal counsel for an unborn child, in fact, that is a sham and an illusion. The real purpose of this legislation is to implement the policy of the Hon. Member, which is to in fact get rid of all abortions in Canada under all circumstances.
Criminal Code
In my view, by prolonging an already unworkable abortion procedure, this Bill indirectly seeks to make legal abortions virtually impossible to obtain in Canada. Because of its perspective, which is fundamentally opposed to freedom of choice, I am rising in opposition to this legislation.
I might say as well, just so that my position on this subject is clear for the record, that I have in fact tabled a Private Members' Bill, Bill C-238, which would remove the provisions of the Criminal Code dealing with abortion and allow this decision to be made by the woman in consultation with her doctor. Certainly, I believe I have an obligation in participating in this important debate to make it very clear where I stand on this question.
Existing Criminal Code provisions generally prohibit abortions unless they are performed in an approved hospital with a therapeutic abortion committee of at least three doctors which has certified that the woman's life or health is likely to be endangered by the continuation of the pregnancy. I note, however, that the establishment of therapeutic abortion committees is not mandatory. In fact, out of a total of 1,300 hospitals in Canada, only 250 have set up committees, and 20 per cent of those hospitals that have established committees do not in fact perform any abortions at all.
Although any decision which is made by a therapeutic abortion committee has very serious implications for the individual woman's future health and welfare, she is not, under Canadian law, entitled to be present at the committee hearing. Nor is she permitted to be represented by counsel at the hearing of the therapeutic abortion committee. The irony of this legislation is that if it were to be adopted, the foetus would have the right to legal representation, but the woman herself would be denied the right to legal representation. Surely the House cannot accept that kind of situation.
Present provisions of the Criminal Code governing abortions have been found to be in contempt of women by panelists in Vancouver, Winnipeg, Toronto, Edmonton and Halifax. These are panelists who are travelling across Canada and reviewing the laws from a woman's perspective. In addition, three juries have acquitted Dr. Henry Morgentaler of abortion-related charges.
Recent Gallup polls indicate that 72 per cent of Canadians call upon the Government to ensure access to safe therapeutic abortions. Recent British polls also indicate extensive public support for the fundamental principle of a woman's right to choose.
The Private Members' Bill of the Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil) ignores these findings and would further restrict and, in practical terms, totally deny the woman's freedom of choice. This is yet another example of the disregard by members of the Conservative caucus of the fundamental concerns of women and their attempt to impose the views of a vociferous and shrill minority on the majority of Canadians.

May 8, 1986
Criminal Code
According to Dr. Nikki Colodny, who performs therapeutic abortions at the Morgentaler Clinic in Toronto, Canadian abortion laws themselves are criminal because they establish a medical delivery system of abortion services which is unnecessarily dangerous and institutionalizes unsafe medical practices. It is women who continue to suffer as a result of this unjust law. The Bill before the House now, by further limiting access to safe therapeutic abortions, simply sanctions unsafe medical practices.
Because of the lack of reasonable access to abortion under the present therapeutic abortion committee system, Canadian women are forced to wait an average of eight weeks between their first appointment and the performance of their abortion. As a result of these delays, Canada has the second highest rate of mid-trimester abortions of all the industrialized nations. By requiring that the fetus be represented by counsel at the therapeutic abortion committee hearing, as proposed by the Hon. Member's Bill, there would simply be further delays, and this would contribute to an even higher rate of mid-trimester abortions and further complications to the woman involved.
Let me point out that therapeutic abortion committees represent the only instance, outside of dealing with mentally incompetent individuals, where a person has three doctors who have never met her, and are not chosen by her, reviewing her private medical records and passing judgment on her health care needs. These doctors are also being asked to make a medical decision about women with whom they have no professional relationship whatsoever. By further complicating and prolonging the already unwieldy and unworkable therapeutic abortion committee process, the Bill before the House would legitimize a system which in effect treats women as somehow mentally incompetent and asks doctors to perform functions for which they have not been properly trained.
As a member of the Subcommittee on Equality Rights of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, I had the opportunity to hear extensive testimony from across Canada on the provisions of the Criminal Code dealing with abortion. In my view, the present Criminal Code provisions governing abortion are one of the most glaring examples of discrimination against women under Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The Code provisions discriminate against women by singling out a particular medical procedure for regulation, which, of course, happens to be carried out on women alone.
The Code provisions are also unequal in their geographic applications, due to discrepancies in hospital policies and procedures. For example, we heard that there were no therapeutic abortion committees in Prince Edward Island. Similarly, women in rural areas or communities in which no therapeutic abortion committees have been set up must travel to other parts of Canada or, in some cases, to the United States to obtain access to abortions. This Bill, which would further restrict a
woman's right to choose, makes a mockery of sexual and economic equality in Canada.
The fact is that the purpose of this Bill is to make abortions illegal. In countries where abortions are illegal, women continue to need and obtain abortions. A further limitation on Canadian women's access to this procedure, therefore, is unlikely to result in a decrease in the number of abortions performed. It will only result in a decrease in the number of safe legal abortions. Any additional limitation on a woman's right to choose, such as that contained in the Bill before the House, would simply assist in recreating the pre-1969 scenario when abortions were completely illegal and women had to resort to back room abortionists. If further laws limiting women's access to abortion are passed in Canada, more and more Canadian women will suffer from the effect of these back room abortions or, indeed, selfinduced abortions by desperate women.
I do not question the goal, which I am sure all Members of the House share, to try to reduce and limit the number of abortions performed in Canada. However, I do not believe that additional prohibitions in the Criminal Code will achieve this end. For this reason amongst others, I emphasize that the policy of the New Democratic Party calls for decriminalization of abortion and the repeal of these provisions from the Criminal Code.
If the Government and the Hon. Member were serious about limiting the number of abortions, they would support positive preventive schemes rather than unrealistic, unworkable, and punitive Criminal Code prohibitions. Constructive measures which could be taken include financial support for family planning and counselling agencies such as Planned Parenthood, conducting research into safer and more effective birth control, introduction of sex education into schools, provision of more information on birth control to young people generally and greater financial and related support services for poor families and single parents.
The Government and this Bill does nothing constructive in the area of family planning. We in the New Democratic Party support the objectives of the Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada in taking steps to reduce the number of unwanted pregnancies. Certainly we will continue to resist legislation such as this which attacks the fundamental freedom of choice of Canadian women.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT RESPECTING LEGAL COUNSEL FOR UNBORN CHILD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to express my views on the Bill presented by the Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands- Canso (Mr. O'Neil). The purpose of the Bill before the House is to have every unborn child represented before the therapeutic abortion committee by State-appointed counsel who would be responsible for upholding the provisions of the Criminal Code. Such a measure would radically change the present system.
May 8, 1986

Mr. Speaker, I shall, if I may, elaborate somewhat on the question to make my colleagues aware of what is at stake. We are talking about abortion. We are talking about the right to life. We are talking about the right to keep a fetus from being brought to term, from completing its nine-month development and being born.
I would like to draw a parallel with ... You know, Mr. Speaker, between 40,000 and 45,000 people die of hunger every day, and most of these are children. Has anyone set up an international or national committee to help these children, to help all these people out of this terrible situation? Has anyone given them a better life than the one they know today? No, Mr. Speaker, because what usually happens is that we spend millions so the media can show us how awful the lives of these people are.
Mr. Speaker, I think we can draw this parallel, because abortion is a fairly complex question. It is a matter where the feelings of the mother come first, because after all, she is the one who bears the fetus, but we must also think of the fetus, because it is a being that has a right to live like any other entity-I don't think we can say: you don't have the right and you do-it is a matter on which Canadian men and women generally tend to let their emotions speak first, and this is quite normal because our emotions are a part of us.
The second reason-today, we would call it a social or economic reason.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I think we must look at the state of our society. Can we allow ... These are the moral questions-not whether we want to set up a committee or not-these are the moral questions our society is asking today.
Do we morally have the right to let a baby come into this world if he or she will be deprived of essential services and care right from birth? Do we morally have the right to let a child be born without parents to raise and educate him or her? Conversely, we might consider this alternative: Do we as civilized Canadian men and women have the right to let a human being die in a society such as ours, a society of plenty, an affluent society , an industrialized society, a society where most men and women own their house and enjoy material wealth? These are two basic questions, Mr. Speaker, questions of principle which transcend any legislation and go far beyond the mere legal purview of the Bill now before the House.
You know, Mr. Speaker, it is convenient to say: We will appoint a lawyer for this, and we will appoint a lawyer for that. Does the Bill provide counsel for the father? Does the Bill provide counsel for the mother? What right, what privilege does any lawyer enjoy to come to the defence of the foetus? What is the position of the foetus, if any? What about the position of the mother? As you know, Mr. Speaker, when an abortion is necessary it has to be done without undue delay, and we all know how very slowly the judicial system works.
I think it is important to consider the context, to realize how serious the matter is, and to keep in mind that the existing
Criminal Code
legislation has authorized therapeutic hospital abortion since 1969.
However, before seeking to improve the legislation as my colleague from Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil) would do, or curtail rights as my colleague from Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) advocates, the basic question should be to ask ourselves how the existing Act is being enforced. We should sit down and consider how the Act is being interpreted. Over the past few years what has been the social evolution of the people who make the decisions, the people who sit on these committees? What criterion guides the people and physicians who sit on a committee responsible for saying yes or no to therapeutic abortions? Just what are their guidelines? The Criminal Code, as prescribed in the Act? Is priority given to health hazards threatening the expectant mother? Or is consideration given to the social environment and the way of life of the pregnant woman?
In my view, it is important, Mr. Speaker, that we stop and look at how complex such a legislation can be, that we stop and discuss and think about how important the life of a human being can be, even though he or she is still unborn, even though in many cases we do not yet know his or her sex, that we stop and think about how important the life of the mother, the life of the father, the social impact on that family are, if we want that everything proceed properly.
I was listening earlier to my colleague for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) who stated that according to a poll, 72 per cent of respondents-although the figure may be slightly less, I think it was 72 per cent, and please correct me if I am wrong-were for maintaining abortion.
Recently I made a survey in my own constituency. The question was quite simple. I asked: "Are you for or against abortion?" And on the bottom line I added: "Comments, if any." Mr. Speaker, I had over 3,000 answers. This is much more than a national survey, as you know, 3,000 answers. And of those 3,000 people, 80 per cent were against abortion. In the majority of cases, reasons were not even given for being against. In some cases, respondents suggested: If we were all in favour of abortion, you might not be there. We have no right to kill a human being. We have no right to put a price on someone's head for the sake of temporary principles, economic principles. Very few people wrote to say: "Mr. Champagne, we support abortion." Very few. Those men and women who wrote and gave me their reasons referred to the ones I indicated earlier-economic reasons, social reasons, that could be termed rational reasons to a certain extent.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it would be useful and interesting, before we decide to have such a legislation passed, before we overload a legislation which is already quite involved in itself since it already rules on the life or death of a human being, since it rules on what will be the future of a human being that cannot defend itself, I say it would be important in the first place to discuss the matter fully, rather than submit it to the House as a piece of legislation or simply enact it, to have the

May 8, 1986
Criminal Code
issue debated on its merits and discussed with those who are mainly involved.
You know, Mr. Speaker, I deeply regret that there are not many women Members in this Elouse. Yet, if there are people who should have their say about this, who should be able to chose, who would be in the best position to give an opinion, 1 honestly believe that it is women, and if I am wrong, I hope that someone will correct me. Yet, when have we seen a panel of women who have been through abortion, women who are for, or against abortion, discuss and develop a policy and determine to what extent it should be applied?
On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, what is now being proposed is that a lawyer be brought in to judge the matter. But to judge what when we do not even know the priorities of the people involved? In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this is carrying principles a bit too far. Instead, we should sit down and listen to people and really look closely at a social problem which is becoming increasingly serious. I think that we would then be able to develop regulations which would not be based simply on legal principles, but rather on human considerations. Indeed, in my opinion, the principle of abortion itself is a human issue.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT RESPECTING LEGAL COUNSEL FOR UNBORN CHILD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to Bill C-254, an Act to amend the Criminal Code to provide for legal counsel for the unborn child at meetings of therapeutic abortion committees.

First, Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Champlain (Mr. Champagne) on his speech. 1 quite agree with him that this problem is extremely difficult for all of us in this House. It is a fundamental issue.
This Bill-

I would now like to say in English that I think that the proposed amendment is flawed in one sense. As the Hon. Member for Champlain (Mr. Champagne) has said, it is flawed in the sense that we cannot bring such an important issue to the floor of the House of Commons in the form of an
amendment which has to be voted upon on the spot without thorough consideration.
Mr. Speaker, from having been in the House for as many years as you have, and having watched the House of Commons for as many years as I have from upstairs on the third floor, I cannot think of two more difficult issues for Members of Parliament, regardless of political stripe, than the issues of capital punishment and abortion. With respect to the issue of capital punishment, I believe the commitment of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to deal with the matter and to allow a free vote on it at some time in the future.
If the matter of abortion ever comes to a vote, as a matter of personal conscience and so that there will be absolutely no question in the minds of my constituents or my colleagues with respect to where I stand on the issue, I oppose abortion. I believe that life begins at the moment of conception. It is my strongly-held view that nothing should interrupt that life short of a medical emergency. If a pregnancy should develop into an emergency which threatens the life of either the mother or the child, then I am not qualified to judge. I am not a doctor. Very few of us in the Chamber are medical practitioners. I think that these situations can only be left to qualified medical practitioners. In my view, then, and only then, does the subject of abortion become a matter of concern between a woman and her doctor. I do not think that any law should govern that type of life and death situation save for the Hippocratic oath. I want to place on the record that, in principle, I am against abortion.
That being said, we have problems with this Bill. As I have said, few subjects are as controversial as is the subject of abortion. Clearly, the deep-seated reasons for the controversy surrounding this issue stem from the often irreconcilable personal choices available in such important, varied areas as morality, religion, sexuality, politics, and family and social life. There is no doubt that we will see a whole spectrum of opinion about something as personal as the matter of abortion. The same is true with respect to the issue of life and death in terms of capital punishment.
Whatever opinion a person has about the current abortion legislation, it is important to know the legal grounds of the issue. Bill C-254 deals with that issue. The reform introduced by Parliament in 1969 rectified an unbearable situation for the medical profession. What exactly was this situation? In what way did the reform change the rules of the game? Is it true, as some believe, that the law-makers chose to liberalize abortion by making it available for all practical purposes on demand? These are the main questions which the Government and all Members of Parliament are desperately attempting to answer.
I would like to give some background on the need for reform. I do not want to go on for too long because I believe my friend, the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Schellenberg), would like to say a few words on this matter. However, I wish to say that there is a real need for reform. Whether a person is for or against the liberalization of the abortion law, there appears to be a consensus regarding the
May 8, 1986

absolute necessity in certain cases of terminating a pregnancy. How in fact can one be opposed to the idea of destroying a foetus when, in the opinion of competent members of the medical profession, the pregnancy truly endangers the life of the mother and could even bring about her immediate death? There are no fewer people today than before 1969 who would prefer to save the life of the mother who may already have children for whom she is responsible than that of the unborn child.
In conclusion, 1 do not think that we as politicians really have the medical qualifications or the moral qualifications to decide whether or not an abortion should be performed, except for the general principle that some of us just do not like the principle of abortion. We want the foetus as a growing human being to live and to enjoy life. Therefore, I think it is up to the doctor, on the basis of the Hippocratic oath, to decide whether the life of the baby or the mother is in danger. It is only up to them and not up to Parliament. We will have to come to grips with this issue at some point in time. I just wish to place on the record where I stand on this issue.
Mir. Ted Schellenberg (Nanaimo-Alberni): Mr. Speaker, I too am honoured to rise this evening to speak on Bill C-254. I would like to thank my colleague, the Hon. Member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott), for allowing me a few minutes. I do not know if I have many minutes in order to get my point across.
What I would like to say is that I agree with what my colleague from Hamilton-Wentworth has said. This is one of those issues that, no matter what we do, we will upset some people. As politicians, we often feel like referees in this business. When we blow the whistle, we upset half the crowd and please the other half. Normally, that breakdown is more like 80/20, or even 90/10, as opposed to 50/50.
I too oppose abortion. However, I also oppose this Bill for a variety of reasons. My colleague from British Columbia, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), who is a member of the NDP, raised some interesting points on this matter when he talked about the lawyers. It is bad enough that politicians have to make these decisions, but when we consider the lawyers, as opposed to doctors, we really get into trouble. Somebody said that when the Constitution was being debated and after the completion of the debate that it would make a great many lawyers a great deal of money over a long period of time. I am afraid that that has turned out to be true. That is similar to this Bill.
How will these lawyers be selected? There is a wide range of opinion in the legal profession. Would this work only be available to lawyers philosophically opposed to abortion? I am also very reluctant to support legislation which would force costs of a substantial nature upon the provinces. The Minister of Social Services, the Minister responsible for the provision of
Adjournment Debate
counsel under this Bill, for each province is endeavouring, I am sure, to reduce costs within his or her own Department in these times of severe fiscal restraint.
Those are some of the problems I have with this Bill. I see that you are indicating my time has almost expired, Mr. Speaker.
I would like to conclude by stating that while the issue will continue to be the subject of debate, and while I commend the Hon. Member for his efforts and concern in this area, the proposed amendment is too flawed to be put forth at this time.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

speechtext:
Last April 25, Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister responsible I asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) whether his Government was trying to get out of meeting its commitments concerning funding of a new French educational television network in Ontario.
The President of the Treasury Board assured me that he would discuss the matter with the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) and provide an explanation for any delay in implementing the agreement.
Here are some of the background facts, Mr, Speaker. As you may recall, in October 1984 the federal Minister of Communications and the Minister of Civic and Cultural Affairs of Ontario began discussions which led to the December 18, 1984 announcement about an agreement in principle with respect to French educational TV services in Ontario.
This agreement in principle, Mr. Speaker, the federal and provincial Governments were bound to earmark up to $3 million a year each over a five-year period for TV Ontario network equipment and operating expenditures.
These monies will serve to increase to 70 hours a week French language programming on the educational television network in Ontario through a satellite cable transmission system.
On June 18, 1985, the Federal Minister of Communications and the Ontario Minister of Citizenship and Culture, Mr. Nick Leluk, announced officially this time a $30 million-

May 8, 1986
Adjournment Debate
subsidy for the funding of this network. According to a press release dated June 18, 1985, the Government of Canada's contribution had been made possible through some Secretary of State programs and funds available from Telefilm Canada for the development of Canadian programming.
Today, over a year and a half later, we have an accumulation of press releases announcing a French language educational television network in Ontario, but no definite or signed agreement, and the province has yet to receive the promised federal contribution. Without this financial contribution from the Federal Government, the province just could not on its own ensure the survival of a French language television network in Ontario.
That is why, on April 25 last, I asked the Minister in this House whether his Government was trying to evade its obligation or whether they would sign the agreement shortly.
On May 1, a few days ago, I wrote to the Minister of Communications to ask him to provide me with a specific answer concerning the said agreement with his provincial counterpart.
Mr. Speaker, I have yet to receive a written reply from the Minister of Communications, but today, in the course of a few telephone calls we made, I was informed that this very morning in Toronto, there was a meeting of federal and provincial representatives for the purpose of negotiating conditions that would be acceptable to both parties.
Mr. Speaker, I hope the negotiations were successful and that this evening, the Parliamentary Secretary who will respond on behalf of the Minister will be able to announce the official signing of the agreement and what the conditions are.
Mr. Speaker, this agreement is particularly important since the survival of French language educational television in Ontario is at stake.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Ottawa- Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) raised an interesting question on April 25, 1986, in relation to the Government's financial contribution to the creation of a French-language educational TV network in Ontario.
